Introduction/Organisation transformation

Development guide

Organisation transformation

An IT department building enterprise systems for several business domains needs more than faster code generation. Leaders need to prepare specialist teams, connect their work across the delivery lifecycle and govern agents within clear quality, security and decision boundaries.

This chapter helps IT leaders plan changes across people, process, culture and technology. A fictional Enterprise Systems Department delivers systems for medical and logistics divisions, using specialist expertise to improve delivery without losing clear accountability.

The focus is AI-assisted enterprise-system delivery and the shared services that support it. AI agents use models and tools to carry out tasks within agreed permissions. Familiarity with IT delivery and responsibility for service decisions is sufficient; detailed configuration stays in the optional reference.

AIHow AI can help in this chapter

Why the operating model needs to change

An IT department can introduce AI tools and still leave business divisions waiting for system changes. In a team organised around specialist functions, work moves from requirements through architecture and development to quality and security review. Faster code generation can enlarge the next queue if those functions remain disconnected or every decision travels upwards.

Start with the enterprise systems and delivery commitments the department owns. Decide how specialists will collaborate, where scarce expertise must be shared and which decisions can be delegated under existing authority. Judge progress through full service costs, responsiveness to business divisions and verified reassignment of specialist capacity.

Use research to frame questions, then measure locally

DORA describes AI as amplifying an organisation's existing strengths and weaknesses. McKinsey found an association between reported AI value and workflow redesign, rather than evidence that redesign caused the results. These findings support examining the operating model; they do not establish a return for an enterprise systems department. [1] [2]

METR's early-2025 study found slower completion among experienced developers working in familiar repositories. Its February 2026 follow-up had selection and time-measurement problems. Neither predicts current departmental performance. Retain the study context in the research detail, and compare local service outcomes with the full costs and conditions of achieving them. [3] [4]

Four areas that change together

The four pillars describe one change in how work gets done. T-shaped staff prepare the context and direct agents; a revised process delegates suitable reviews; the culture supports useful adoption and informed challenge; technology enforces quality, compliance and human decision boundaries. Each example below applies its pillar to that same arrangement.

  • People: build specialist-owned context and T-shaped capability to specify, direct and integrate agent-assisted work.
  • Process: replace validated lower-impact human review duties with agent reviews, while retaining people at key gates.
  • Culture: prepare for agents as part of work, with source checking and open reporting of variable or invented outputs.
  • Technology: enforce context, review scope, quality and compliance controls, human gates and recovery.
Worked exampleFictional caseChoose an enterprise IT delivery problemConnect specialist delivery work to the enterprise systems business divisions need.

The fictional Enterprise Systems Department designs, builds, integrates and maintains twelve enterprise systems for four business divisions:

  • Medical Services
  • Medical Administration
  • Logistics Operations
  • Logistics Planning

These systems support medical administration, inventory and distribution. Product managers work with business owners to define what the systems need to achieve. The IT team delivers and maintains the systems, while the business divisions run the services they support.

The department has 24 IT staff working in six specialist roles:

  • Four product managers
  • Three architects
  • Ten developers
  • Three quality reviewers
  • Two security reviewers
  • Two cyber managers

Staff have traditionally developed their skills within their own speciality, passing work to the next team when their part is complete. Changes often wait for the same few architects or reviewers, and unclear requirements lead to repeated questions between teams. Domain experts work in the business divisions, while shared teams provide platform services.

The department head wants specialists to contribute across more of the delivery process with help from agents. Staff will prepare the knowledge agents need and practise using them beyond their usual tasks. Agents will take over suitable routine reviews, while people keep control of key decisions. The examples below follow this change across the four pillars and ask whether it improves delivery within the department's staffing and full service costs.

All events, roles, dates and figures in this case are illustrative.

People: develop T-shaped skills for work with agents

Specialist expertise becomes a foundation for broader work with agents. A T-shaped practitioner retains depth in a discipline and develops breadth across business context, task specification, agent supervision and integration. The transition changes what staff can undertake with assistance, rather than asking them to rely only on their previous speciality.

Turn specialist and domain knowledge into usable context

Each role should help make its knowledge available to agents as current, task-relevant context: the information supplied or retrieved for the task. This includes business meaning and organisational constraints as well as technical instructions. Work with the business divisions to verify domain facts, and assign owners to keep the material current. Context engineering is the discipline of selecting and maintaining that information. [13]

Prepare staff to specify an outcome, select the relevant context, delegate bounded work and judge the returned result. A product manager can explore an implementation question with an agent and then involve an architect; a developer can prepare an initial test proposal for a quality reviewer. Broader contribution does not transfer the specialist's approval authority.

Assess that broader practice through completed work, including flawed agent outputs and missing organisational context. Product, architecture, development, quality, security and cyber management retain distinct judgement. Protect independent human decisions at key gates while developing the ability to coordinate agents across a larger part of delivery.

Worked exampleFictional caseBuild context and practise a broader delivery roleApply T-shaped development to the same enterprise-system work, using specialist knowledge to direct agents.

The team starts with a change to a logistics system. Each specialist helps prepare a shared set of reference material for agents to use. The business owner confirms the meaning of the workflow terms, including the distinction between “ready for review” and “approved for release”. Each role maintains the material it knows best:

  • Product managers: business terms, user workflows, intended outcomes and examples of acceptable behaviour.
  • Architects: system boundaries, integration contracts and recorded design decisions.
  • Developers: repository guidance, coding conventions and verified implementation patterns.
  • Quality reviewers: acceptance cases, failure cases and expected results.
  • Security reviewers: threats, data-access rules and required security evidence.
  • Cyber managers: current organisational control requirements, escalation routes and incident responsibilities, confirmed with the people responsible.

During a coached session, a product manager asks an agent to use this material to propose the change and suggest how to test it. An architect checks the integration assumptions, and a quality reviewer checks the expected behaviour. A developer then directs an agent to draft a small part of the implementation and prepare evidence for review.

This is how the team begins to develop T-shaped skills. Staff use their specialist knowledge to guide agents while contributing to work they would previously have handed over. They still involve the relevant specialist when a task reaches the limits of their expertise or authority.

When an agent follows an obsolete release instruction, the coach asks the team to trace the mistake to its source. The person responsible updates the reference material and records a new version. The team repeats the task and compares the result with the current rule. The coach records how well staff select context, delegate work, spot errors and use the results.

The department head sets aside four hours a week for each participant during the first month and funds time to maintain the reference material. Product managers record which delivery work must wait. The later outcome review checks whether this investment helps staff contribute more widely and respond faster to business needs.

AIHow AI can help

Agents can extend a team member's contribution by drafting proposals, code, tests or review findings using the curated context. The team member specifies the task and integrates the result, involving the relevant specialist at the agreed boundary. Retain context versions, review findings and demonstrated competence.

What you do as a leader

Agree development plans that combine specialist depth with domain knowledge, context ownership and practical agent supervision. Fund maintenance and coached cross-role work alongside existing delivery commitments.

Judge readiness through observed delegation and checking, and use the role reference to retain clear expertise and authority. Track whether broader contribution improves productivity and agility without treating released time as a cash saving.

Process: delegate routine reviews and retain human control at key gates

Redesign the work allocated to people and agents, rather than adding AI to every existing human review. A validated agent can take over an agreed lower-impact review task, releasing specialist time for consequential judgement. Choose that task by its impact, evidence and recoverability, not by assuming a professional role is unimportant.

  1. Define the delegated review. Name its scope, authoritative context, criteria, permitted outcome and exclusions. Use deterministic checks for fixed fields and formats; an agent can assess meaning or consistency within that bounded task.
  2. Validate before replacing the routine human step. Compare repeated agent runs with qualified reviewers' expected findings on ordinary, flawed and out-of-scope cases. Agree acceptable errors, required referrals and monitoring before the agent becomes the designated reviewer.
  3. Retain people at key gates. Keep the applicable human decisions on material requirements or architecture, quality and security acceptance, residual-risk exceptions and production release. Missing evidence, uncertainty or a scope breach sends work to the named person.

The process owner authorises the delegated task under existing powers and remains accountable for its operation. Once validated and authorised, the routine step can complete without a person repeating every agent review. Audit samples, monitor missed findings and added rework, and restore the human step when the agreed stop criteria are met. Agent review completion is not release approval.

Worked exampleFictional caseReplace a routine human review within a tested boundaryShow an agent taking over a lower-impact review while people retain the decisive gates.

A member of staff currently checks every change pack before it reaches the specialist reviewers. This initial readiness check asks whether the terminology, requirements, tests and supporting evidence agree. The process owner proposes giving an agent this task for predefined routine system changes. Changes to material business rules, access rights or compliance exceptions will still go to specialists.

Quality and security leads agree the criteria and the cases that need a person. The agent uses the reference material prepared by the specialists, together with the change pack and its evidence links. Ordinary automated checks verify fixed fields, links and revisions. The agent checks the meaning and consistency of the content, then records a result or asks for a correction. It cannot change the approval rules.

Before changing the process, reviewers label thirty test cases: 24 routine changes the agent may review and six that require referral because evidence is missing or the work falls outside its scope. The first configuration confuses “ready for review” with release approval, so the team corrects it and repeats the assessment. Across three runs, the revised workflow produces these results:

  • All six cases requiring a person are referred in every run.
  • No output claims that release has been approved.
  • Among the eligible routine changes, one, two and one cases are referred unnecessarily in the respective runs.

The results meet the agreed limits: no missed required referral and at most two unnecessary referrals per run. Reviewers retain the automated check results separately from the agent's findings. These fictional results support a trial within the tested scope; future performance still needs monitoring.

The authorised process owner puts the agent in charge of that routine check. Staff no longer repeat it for every eligible change. Workflow controls check the change category and allow the agent to record only its review result. When a logistics change pack uses the wrong status term, the agent returns it for correction. A request involving live medical data goes to the security and data owners.

People still make material design decisions and the required quality, security and release decisions. The process owner keeps the evaluation and review records, including referrals and the versions of context and configuration used. Human sampling and monitoring for failed checks can trigger a return to the former human review step. The trial includes this supervision and any rework when calculating costs and capacity released.

AIHow AI can help

A review agent can complete a validated routine review instead of its former human checker within the authorised scope. Relevant specialists assess its suitability, monitor its errors and handle referrals. Keep deterministic checks, agent judgements and human gate decisions identifiable in the record.

What you do as a leader

Identify which routine review duties can move to agents and which key gates retain human decisions. Agree evaluation and stop criteria with the control owners, then obtain the applicable authorisation for the changed workflow.

Remove the duplicated human routine step only within the validated scope. Retain accountable owners and exception routes, and measure the change in specialist capacity, queue time, quality and full cost.

Culture: make agent use normal while keeping judgement and challenge

Prepare people to include agents in ordinary task planning, execution and review, and to question their results openly. Leaders should support useful experimentation and disclosure of failures, rather than rewarding tool usage or accepting generated output because it sounds confident. Senior accountability continues as some routine tasks move to agents.

Language-model outputs can be non-deterministic: repeated runs can produce different answers even with the same inputs. They can also hallucinate, generating unsupported facts, rules or conclusions. Missing organisational context can leave an agent using assumptions that do not fit the department; relevant context helps ground the task but does not guarantee correctness. [14] [15]

Build habits that make the uncertainty manageable: use current context, distinguish a proposal from evidence and record what remains unknown. Encourage staff to report a mistaken result and improve the shared context or evaluation cases. The validated routine-review boundary governs delegated work; key human decisions still need the appropriate evidence and accountable judgement.

DORA connects trust and information flow with stronger performance and identifies a clear organisational position on AI use as a supporting capability. Explain where agent use is expected, where it is bounded and how staff can challenge it without pressure to demonstrate a speed gain. [7] [8]

Worked exampleFictional caseLearn to work with a useful but fallible agentConnect acceptance of agents to source checking, shared context and supported challenge.

Before handing over the routine review, the team practises with the same logistics change. A team member asks an agent how the change should progress, initially without the department's reference material. Two runs suggest different approval routes. One invents a mandatory approval board. The product manager and cyber manager check the current delegation record and find no basis for that board.

The team then supplies the reference material and asks the agent to link its conclusions to those sources and flag any missing authority. The next answer follows the correct route, but another run still confuses “ready for review” with release approval. The quality reviewer records the error and adds it to the evaluation cases. The team sees that context helps the agent answer, but does not make every answer reliable.

The department head backs the person who questioned the output. Staff continue using the agent for useful drafting while the team improves the instructions and carries the findings into the routine-review evaluation. The review owner can withdraw the delegated task if it later meets the agreed failure criteria. People remain responsible for decisions at the key gates.

At the next fortnightly retrospective, specialist leads discuss what helped and what needed correction:

  • Which outputs were useful, and where did they save work?
  • Which errors or missing context affected the result?
  • How much supervision was needed, and what remains unresolved?

The team updates its reference material and assigns follow-up actions. These discussions help staff make agents part of everyday work while continuing to question their results and report limitations.

AIHow AI can help

Agents can suggest approaches and questions for the team to discuss. Staff compare variable or unsupported answers with organisational sources, record errors and improve the context or controls. Leaders support adoption by backing useful delegation and justified challenge.

What you do as a leader

Set expectations for everyday agent use and for reporting its limitations. Give staff time to practise, maintain organisational context and raise contradictory evidence without being labelled resistant to change.

Keep human accountability visible as routine work is delegated. Use feedback alongside error, rework and queue records to decide whether the working arrangement needs correction.

Technology: govern context, delegated reviews and key gates

The technical environment should enforce the roles assigned to agents in the operating model. Its harness combines instructions and context access with tools, permissions and checks. A prompt asking an agent to follow policy does not enforce that policy or grant authority.

IMDA recommends bounded agent risk, human accountability and lifecycle controls; OWASP recommends limiting functionality, permissions and autonomy, with authorisation enforced in connected systems. Apply these principles to context ownership, routine review delegation and the human gates the department retains. [5] [6] [9]

  • Controlled context: provide approved domain and organisational sources with owners, versions and access limits. Detect missing or stale required context and route the task for correction.
  • Bounded execution: enforce which tasks an agent can review, which systems it can change and which decisions require a person. An agent cannot promote its own task to a lower-risk category or approve a human gate.
  • Quality and compliance evidence: evaluate repeated runs, retain original results and trace findings to the applicable requirements. Policy owners interpret obligations and the authorised people accept residual risk; an agent's compliance label is not that decision.
  • Sustained operation: monitor errors and referrals, test stopping and recovery, and reassess relevant model, context, policy or tool changes. Fund the maintenance and support.

The technical delivery reference retains implementation detail. Leaders commission evidence that the configured controls support the proposed allocation of work, including the routine human step being replaced.

Worked exampleFictional caseEnforce the review boundary and preserve human gatesApply the harness to the same context and routine review introduced in People and Process.

Architects and security reviewers configure the agent for the routine readiness check. It can retrieve approved reference material and relevant change evidence, then write its findings to the review record. Repository and workflow controls limit which change categories it can review. The agent cannot widen its own scope or record a human approval.

Each key gate requires the authorised person to record a decision under their own identity. An agent's claim that a change is approved cannot open that gate. Cyber managers confirm the applicable controls with policy owners, and the shared platform team records the model, instruction and context versions used for each run. The record also retains source links and original test results.

If required context is missing, a decision claim lacks support or a change falls outside the agreed scope, the workflow refers it to a named person. Specialists test these controls through repeated runs:

  • An eligible routine change receives a readiness result without someone repeating the same check.
  • A stale policy source or missing evidence blocks completion and triggers referral.
  • An attempt by the agent to record quality, security or production-release approval is denied.
  • The team can stop the agent, revoke its access and return the review task to a person while retaining the records.

Reviewers compare the successful and blocked actions with the agreed criteria and retain the results. The department head funds the review service and its monitoring within the scope those tests support. A proposed connection to live medical records remains outside that scope because its control evidence is incomplete.

The service owner repeats the relevant evaluation when the model, context or policy changes materially. Each review can be traced to the configuration assessed and the people responsible for exceptions, policy interpretation and final decisions. The controls therefore enforce the agent's role through the surrounding systems.

AIHow AI can help

Agents can help prepare context inventories, review criteria, configurations and test cases. Specialists compare them with authoritative requirements and actual system behaviour. Use controlled sources, enforced permissions and original results to establish the supported scope.

What you do as a leader

Fund the controlled context, evaluation and workflow enforcement needed for T-shaped staff and delegated reviews. Name owners for quality, security, compliance interpretation, support and human decisions at key gates.

Approve an expansion proposal only when evidence supports the new tasks and data access. Preserve monitoring, stop conditions and the ability to return delegated work to people.

Ownership: sustain shared capability across divisions

Enterprise systems depend on shared architecture, assurance and delivery platforms. Product managers coordinate business priorities; architects maintain system and integration direction; quality and security reviewers maintain their assurance criteria. Cyber managers coordinate cyber oversight and incident readiness. Map each responsibility to existing authority and retain business ownership of domain requirements and acceptance.

Keep specialist capacity, IT delivery commitments, escalation contacts and review dates alongside the funding plan. The shared service ownership reference provides the detailed maintenance matrix. Shared capacity can reduce duplication, but it can also become a new queue if leaders fund adoption without sufficient support.

Separate evaluation of a development agent from tests of the system it helps build. Evaluation cases are sample tasks with expected results used to judge a tool against agreed criteria. If a delivered service itself uses AI, assign ownership of its behavioural evaluation and operational monitoring as well.

Next step: agree a cross-division ownership and resource record with the service and budget owners. Resolve gaps in maintenance, assurance or support before widening the service commitment.

Review outcomes and decide the next investment

Use a bounded organisational trial to test how the specialist IT teams deliver across the selected business divisions. Establish the enterprise-system scope, comparison periods, populations and targets before starting. Finance, human resources and service owners should reconcile the results against underlying cost, work and queue records.

  1. Agree the comparison. Name the supported services, request types, complexity bands, divisions and workforce. Retain differences in demand, risk and experience that limit comparison.
  2. Cost the complete service. Include staff time, assurance, shared platforms, model charges, transition, training, dual running, support and incident work. Count costs once and include work that remains unresolved.
  3. Measure responsiveness across divisions. Track request-to-acceptance time alongside open queues, age and overdue work. A completed-work median excludes requests still waiting.
  4. Verify workforce reassignment. Compare routine effort, then trace released hours to actual assignments and completed work. Keep estimates, verified capacity use and changes in payroll or establishment separate.
  5. Record an investment decision. Judge the agreed targets and control evidence, retain unresolved findings and assign corrective work, resources and a next review date.
Worked exampleFictional caseUse the outcome record to decide investmentCompare full costs, divisional queues and verified staff reassignment.

The Enterprise Systems Department compares April–June 2026 with July–September. Both periods cover the same twelve enterprise systems, four business divisions and 24 IT specialists. The comparison counts completed small system-change requests, using the same agreed mix of request types and complexity in both quarters. Acceptance means the authorised product or business owner has confirmed the defined delivery result with the required quality and security evidence; reopened work counts once after final acceptance.

Cost records cover the full IT service portfolio, including unresolved delivery work, system maintenance and allocated shared-platform support. Completed requests are observed for 14 calendar days after acceptance, through 14 October for the review quarter. On 19 October, the department head reviews the record with product managers and specialist leads. Finance, human resources and business representatives help check the findings.

Cost effectiveness: compare the full service cost

Illustrative quarterly IT service costs and accepted changes

Recurring service costsS$1,200,000S$1,260,000
Transition costsS$0S$180,000
Full service costsS$1,200,000S$1,440,000
Accepted system-change requests2,4003,000
Full IT cost per accepted changeS$500S$480

Recurring costs include staff and assurance costs, together with platform and model services. Maintenance and support are included, as is incident work. The S$180,000 transition cost funds training and temporary cover, alongside setup and dual running. Finance reconciles these allocations without counting staff time twice.

The agreed target is a 10% reduction in full IT cost per accepted change: at most S$450 against S$500. The result is S$1,440,000 ÷ 3,000 = S$480, a 4% reduction, so the target is missed. Total quarterly cost rises by S$240,000, or 20%. The S$420 recurring-only figure excludes transition and is not the full result.

Agility: inspect the divisions and unfinished work

The target is a median system-change request-to-acceptance time of at most seven working days in each division, with no increase in requests still open beyond 14 working days. Timing starts when the IT change request is recorded and includes specialist and management waiting. Medians describe completed changes; the aged queue is a quarter-end snapshot of unresolved IT changes, including requests received earlier.

Accepted IT changes rise from 2,400 to 3,000, but changes for Medical Services still miss the time target. The aged IT change queue grows from 50 to 60, with medical-system requests rising from 30 to 46. Logistics-system delivery improves on both measures. Leaders investigate the medical-system delivery delays and specialist capacity before claiming improved responsiveness across all client divisions. These figures measure IT delivery, not medical or logistics operations.

Manpower optimisation: verify where capacity went

Work records for the same 24 IT specialists show routine delivery coordination and evidence-preparation effort falling from 7,200 to 6,000 person-hours. This releases an estimated 1,200 hours during the quarter; it does not remove the need for specialist judgement. The target is to verify that at least 80% of those hours have been used for other useful work.

  • 540 hours are traced to completed product discovery and architecture reviews for medical-system changes.
  • 360 hours are traced to completed regression-test and integration improvements for logistics systems.
  • 300 hours have no verified replacement-work record and remain unresolved.

Managers and the human-resources lead verify 900 ÷ 1,200 = 75% reassignment, below the 80% target. The 900 hours are part of the 1,200, not an additional saving. Payroll and staffing levels have not fallen. The completed work and salary costs remain in their existing service records; converting these hours to another cash benefit would double count them.

Quality, security and authority remain conditions

The accountable IT and business owners retain acceptance, follow-up and control records with no unresolved required failure in the current supported delivery scope. That finding does not establish readiness for the proposed live medical-data connection, whose control evidence remains incomplete. The combined changes to learning, review, culture, governance and tools mean the comparison cannot attribute the results to AI alone. Leaders assess the changes together using the checked outcome record, including the costs of supervision, evaluation and correction.

Completed leadership decision: continue and correct, with no expansion

On 19 October, the department head uses the existing budget and service authorities to continue the currently supported arrangements for one further quarter, within a S$1,260,000 recurring service allocation. No expansion allocation or broader agent access is authorised. The gains justify continuing within the current scope while the team addresses the missed targets. The cost and workforce results, together with the medical-system queue, do not support expansion at this review.

  • Finance and product managers reconcile full costs and demand mix by 30 November, retaining transition and support costs.
  • Product managers, architects and reviewer leads examine aged medical-system changes and specialist handoff delays, agree priority and review-capacity changes within the allocation, and review the queue weekly with business representatives.
  • Human resources and line managers verify the unresolved 300 hours and agree actual replacement assignments by 30 November.
  • The cyber manager, security reviewer and medical data owner retain the live-data proposal outside the authorised scope pending evidence and the applicable approval.

Corrective work uses existing capacity and displaces lower-priority work explicitly agreed with product managers and business-division representatives; it is not free additional capacity. The next leadership review is 18 January 2027, after the next quarter and its 14-day follow-up ending 14 January. Leaders will reconsider funding and scope against the same definitions, targets and required controls.

Decide whether to expand, restrict, stop or keep testing

Agree the decision rules before starting. Continuation of a supported service, a further experiment and expansion of agent permissions are distinct decisions.

  • Expand when the agreed outcome targets and required controls support the proposed divisions and uses, with funded expertise and support. Check full costs, unresolved queues and verified reassignment before extending commitments.
  • Restrict when evidence supports only some tasks, divisions or permissions. Retain useful supported services, exclude unsupported uses and assign corrective work before reconsidering them.
  • Stop the affected use when a required control cannot be maintained, serious failures require it or the evaluated cost and support burden cannot be justified. The authorised owner removes access and returns work to a supported arrangement.
  • Keep testing when a specific question or revised arrangement needs evidence. Fund a bounded extension within existing limits, identify what it will resolve and set an end date. Continuing existing services does not authorise a new agent use.

Stop affected actions immediately if an agreed stop condition occurs, and follow the response and recovery procedure. Reassess material changes to models, permissions or workflow. Do not use a department-wide average to offset a failed control or an unsupported domain.

AIHow AI can help

AI can draft comparisons from approved finance, workforce and queue records using the agreed definitions. Finance checks cost allocation; service owners check completed and unresolved populations; human resources checks reassignment evidence. Retain reconciled results, uncertainty and the authorised leadership decision.

Next step: agree a departmental change brief covering service priorities, workforce preparation, assurance and delegation, agent boundaries, full costs and review criteria. Name the owners who will supply the outcome evidence and the authority that can change investment or scope.

Delivery reference: evidence leaders commission

Use these optional references with delivery and control specialists when commissioning evidence. They describe detailed work supporting the leadership decisions above; they are not a technical curriculum for every leader.

Role competencies, skill breadth and accountable delegation

The six role examples match the fictional IT department. They illustrate continuing specialisms and additional AI-assisted responsibilities; map actual duties and approval powers to local arrangements. Product management, quality review, security review and cyber management retain distinct purposes. Where product management and product ownership are separate, agree acceptance authority explicitly.

For interface work, design tokens are named values for colour, typography and spacing. A designer could supply these for a medical-administration or logistics interface so generated screens follow the agreed design. They guide presentation; they do not test data-access permissions.

Prompt injection is an attempt to redirect an agent using instructions in untrusted content. A synthetic domain document could contain text asking an agent to ignore its brief; the security reviewer can use that case to test the boundary. Permitted data access remains a separate control.

Evaluation cases assess the development tool using representative tasks and expected outcomes. Maintain ordinary and deliberately difficult cases, including an omitted data-access rule, so overall success cannot hide a critical failure.

The case obtains platform engineering and operational support from shared platform teams outside its team of 24 IT staff. Agree those teams' capacity and responsibilities and include their cost allocation. Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) automate build, test and delivery steps; shared platform teams maintain those foundations with the application specialists. Release and risk decisions follow existing authorities.

Multi-agent orchestration coordinates dependent or parallel tasks across several agents, then integrates their results. If several agents divide a service change and its tests, a named person still needs to integrate and independently review the results against the brief. Orchestration is an optional delivery specialism with time for review and recovery.

The delegation diagram uses the same six IT specialisms as the case. Choose the accountable owner and independent reviewers according to the task, expertise and authority; the diagram is not a staffing ratio or permission to merge review responsibilities.

The PRD and TRD guidance explains the product requirements document, which describes required outcomes, and technical requirements document, which records how the system will deliver them. Preparation and approval depend on the applicable workflow. Follow the Eitri planning steps when using that implementation.

Task permissions, evidence and authorised decisions

The decision diagram below shows retained human gates. A validated routine agent review can complete under prior authorisation before those gates; the diagram does not add a person to every delegated review.

Code review covers evidence for code changes. Data access, deployment and external communications need controls at their own execution points, including when they occur outside a merge request.

Suggested capabilities and how to check them
CapabilityPractical check
Relevant contextGive the tool current requirements and approved reference material; record their versions and restrict access to what the task needs.
Identity and permissionsUse scoped credentials or delegated access that preserves the user’s authority limits. Check that unauthorised actions are denied.
Isolated executionSeparate experimental work from shared systems. Limit tool access, execution time and spending.
VerificationRun tests against acceptance criteria and retain the results. If AI assesses the work, compare its findings with qualified reviewers using the method below.
Action recordsRecord changes, tool calls, versions and outcomes with appropriate access and retention controls; avoid unnecessary sensitive content.
RecoveryTest stopping a run, revoking access and restoring affected state. Identify actions that cannot be undone.

Assess an automated reviewer before relying on it

The check owner selects routine and higher-risk cases within the proposed task scope and agrees acceptable errors before testing. Qualified reviewers assess the original evidence against the same criteria, independently of the AI assessment. Compare missed defects, unsupported findings and unresolved disagreements; retain cases, versions, expected and observed results, reviewer findings and the suitability decision.

Permit only the use supported by those criteria. If the automated reviewer misses a required data-access defect, a high overall agreement rate does not make it suitable for that check. Keep specialist review or restrict the automated use while the defect is investigated.

DORA associates useful internal platforms and access to relevant internal data with stronger AI benefits. Improve context and platform quality while retaining task-specific access limits. [8]

Build, harden and operate the delivery path

  • CI/CD pipelines: maintain repeatable builds, tests, security checks and deployment stages, with task-limited credentials and retained results. Demonstrate that a failed check blocks progress and rehearse rollback. Follow the EDS pipeline stages when applying that workflow.
  • Infrastructure as code: describe resources and configuration in reviewed, version-controlled files. For a departmental service, these could describe a separate test environment and its access settings. Infrastructure hardening means reducing exposure through agreed identity, network, secrets and patching controls. Retain checks, detect configuration drift from the agreed state and test restoration from backups where needed.
  • Operations and application health: developers and platform engineers collect metrics, logs and traces and check important user journeys. Agree service health targets for availability, latency, errors and resource capacity. Test alerts to a named responder and maintain diagnosis, escalation and recovery instructions.

AI can draft pipeline definitions, infrastructure changes and runbooks. Review generated changes and test them in isolation before authorised promotion. Agree separately who can deploy, change production infrastructure and respond to incidents. This guide maps practices to suggested contributors; actual ownership follows local operating arrangements.

State whether the cases assess a development tool or an AI capability in the product; investigate gaps and rerun checks after relevant changes.

Maintain contacts, capacity, deputy or support route, funding and review dates alongside this record. Assessments of a development tool and evaluations of AI behaviour in a delivered product need their own scope, cases and named owners.

Delivery-level pilot measures supporting the leadership review

Use these task-level measures to diagnose the service results. The leadership record additionally needs complete portfolio costs, divisional queues and verified workforce reassignment. Task effort alone does not establish those outcomes.

Suggested pilot scorecard: agree targets before the trial
MeasureWhat to record and check
Tasks comparedDescribe the scope, difficulty and risk of each task type, participants’ experience and familiarity with the repository. Count baseline and trial attempts, including failures, and explain any differences that weaken the comparison.
Useful resultsRecord which results met the acceptance criteria and what shows they helped the intended user. Keep links to tests, review findings or user observations.
Time to an accepted resultMeasure elapsed time from the agreed start to acceptance, including waiting. Record active human effort separately so that a shorter wait is not mistaken for less work.
Review effortRecord time spent checking requirements, generated work and test evidence. Include specialist reviews and repeated review rounds.
Corrections and failed attemptsRecord time spent fixing rejected outputs, rerunning the tool and recovering from failures. Include effort spent on work that never reached acceptance.
Defects and control failuresTrack defects found after acceptance over the agreed observation period. Record severity, user impact, failed security or other required checks, incidents and recovery results. Examine each serious failure individually.
Readiness to run and support the serviceFor changes affecting delivery or a running service, record pipeline failures, infrastructure security findings, availability, response times and errors. Compare alert response and recovery results with agreed targets. Name the operational owner and record gaps before expanding.
Total costInclude tool and model charges, infrastructure, pipeline and monitoring services, setup, training, human work, shared harness maintenance, evaluation, support and incidents. Include failed attempts and count each cost once. Report both total cost and cost per accepted result.
Participants’ experienceAsk about mental effort, interruptions, learning and confidence in questioning AI output. Compare feedback with observed work and requests for help; fewer reported problems may mean problems went unnoticed.

Keep denominators and periods with each result. Divide all included task effort, including abandoned attempts, by accepted results. Count each person's effort once, retain total cost separately and do not infer a cash saving or shorter waiting time from an effort change alone.

Research detail behind the takeaways

McKinsey's November 2025 survey found its AI high-performer group nearly three times as likely as others to report fundamental workflow redesign. That group reported significant AI value and an AI contribution of at least 5% to earnings before interest and taxes. These self-reported business associations do not establish causation or predict departmental delivery outcomes. Earnings are part of the source's definition, not an objective for the fictional department. [2]

METR's early-2025 randomised study involved 16 experienced open-source developers completing 246 tasks in familiar repositories. Allowing AI increased completion time by 19%, despite participants estimating that it saved time. This is a historical result for those tools, tasks and participants. In February 2026, METR reported selection effects and time-measurement problems that made follow-up data unreliable for estimating current productivity gains. Neither supplies a forecast for an enterprise systems department. [3] [4]
